1Assignment 1

Exercise 1. (10 points) In this exercise, we want to study the action for gravitational waves. Our starting point is the Einstein equations for the gravitational field gμν​(x) identified with the spacetime metric,1Rμν​−21​gμν​R=0,(1)where we used the following notations:

•

Ricci scalar: R=gμνRμν​,

•

Ricci tensor: Rμν​=Rμρνρ​,

•

Riemann tensor: Rσμνρ​=∂μ​Γσνρ​−∂ν​Γσμρ​+Γμαρ​Γνσα​−Γναρ​Γμσα​,

•

Christoffel symbols: Γνρμ​=21​gμσ(∂ρ​gσν​+∂ν​gσρ​−∂σ​gνρ​).

The metric gμν​(x) is assumed symmetric and non-degenerate, and we denote gμν(x) the inverse metric, i.e.gμν(x)gνρ​(x)=δρμ​=gρν​(x)gνμ(x).(2)

1.

We consider a small perturbation around the flat metric gμν​(x)=ημν​+hμν​(x), derive the linearized equations of motion (at order in O(h)). (2 points)

2.

Let h=hμμ​=ημνhμν​, we consider the Fierz-Pauli action for the symmetric tensor hμν​(x), S[h]=∫d4x[−41​∂ρ​hμν​∂ρhμν+21​∂ρ​hμν​∂νhρμ+41​∂ρh∂ρ​h−21​∂ρ​h∂μ​hμρ](3)Show that the Euler-Lagrange equations reproduce the previous linearized equations of motion for hμν​ (2 points).

3.

Compute the fields Πμν​ canonically conjugate to hμν​. (1 point)

4.

Compute the energy-momentum tensor associated to the Fierz-Pauli action. Deduce the Hamiltonian. (2 points)

5.

Show that the theory is invariant under the transformation hμν​(x)→hμν​(x)+∂μ​Vν​(x)+∂ν​Vμ​(x). (3 points)

Solution:

1. We compute the expansion at order O(h) of the Ricci scalar and Ricci tensor,Γνρμ​Rμνρσ​Rμν​R​=21​ημσ(∂ρ​hσν​+∂ν​hσρ​−∂σ​hνρ​)+O(h2),=21​(∂ρ​∂ν​hμσ​+∂μ​∂σ​hρν​−∂ρ​∂μ​hνσ​−∂ν​∂σ​hρμ​)+O(h2),=21​(∂σ​∂ν​hμσ​+∂σ​∂μ​hνσ​−∂μ​∂ν​h−□hμν​)+O(h2),=∂μ​∂ν​hμν−□h,​(4)with h=hμμ​. Thus, at first order, Einstein’s equation becomes∂σ​∂ν​hμσ​+∂σ​∂μ​hνσ​−∂μ​∂ν​h−□hμν​−ημν​∂ρ​∂σ​hρσ+ημν​□h=0.(5)

2. Let’s rewrite the Lagrangian density as follows,L=ημμ′ηνν′ηρρ′(−41​∂ρ​hμν​∂ρ′​hμ′ν′​+21​∂ρ​hμν​∂ν′​hρ′μ′​+41​∂ρ′​hμμ′​∂ρ​hνν′​−21​∂ρ​hνν′​∂μ​hμ′ρ′​)(6)Obviously, we have ∂L/∂hαβ​=0, so let’s compute∂(∂γ​hαβ​)∂L​​=−41​(∂γhαβ+∂γhαβ)+21​(∂βhγα+∂αhβγ)+41​(ηαβ∂γh+ηαβ∂γh)−21​(ηαβ∂μ​hμγ+ηγα∂βh)=−21​∂γhαβ+21​∂βhγα+21​∂αhβγ+21​ηαβ∂γh−21​ηαβ∂μ​hμγ−21​ηαγ∂βh.​(7)The Euler-Lagrange equation∂γ​∂(∂γ​hαβ​)∂L​=0(8)gives−21​□hαβ+21​∂γ​∂βhγα+21​∂γ​∂αhβγ+21​ηαβ□h−21​ηαβ∂γ​∂σ​hσγ−21​∂α∂βh=0(9)Let’s apply 2ηαμ​ηβν​ to this equation, using the fact that hμν​ is symmetric we recover−□hμν​+∂σ​∂ν​hμσ​+∂σ​∂μ​hνσ​+ημν​□h−ημν​∂ρ​∂σ​hρσ−∂μ​∂ν​h=0.(10)

3. It is just a matter of applying the formula,Παβ=∂h˙αβ​∂L​=−21​h˙αβ+21​(∂αh0β+∂βh0α)+21​ηαβ(h˙−∂μ​h0μ)−21​ηα0∂βh.(11)

4. Again, we just apply the formula,Tμν​=∂(∂μ​hαβ​)∂L​∂νhαβ​−Lημν=21​(−∂μhαβ∂νhαβ​+2∂αhμβ∂νhαβ​+∂μh∂νh−∂ρ​hμρ∂νh−∂αh∂νhαμ​)−Lημν.​(12)andH=T00−L=−21​h˙αβh˙αβ​+h˙αβ​∂αh0β+21​h˙2−21​h˙∂α​h0α−h˙μα∂α​h−L.(13)

5. There are two options, either show that the equations of motions are invariant (easier), or show that the Lagrangian is invariant up to a total divergence. We will take the second option here, which is a rather tedious calculation. For simplicity, we split the Lagrangian density into two parts,L=L1​+L2​,L1​=21​∂ρ​hμν​(∂νhρμ−21​∂ρhμν),L2​=21​∂ρ​h(21​∂ρh−∂μ​hμρ).(14)Let’s start with the terms linear in V, after some cancelations, we find the following variations,δL1(1)​δL2(1)​​=∂ρ​hμν∂μ​∂ν​Vρ=∂ρ​(hμν∂μ​∂ν​Vρ)−hμν∂μ​∂ν​∂ρ​Vρ,=21​∂ρh∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ−21​∂ρh□Vρ​−∂μ​(hμρ)∂ρ​∂ν​Vν,=21​(∂ρ(h∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ)−h∂μ​□Vμ)−21​(∂ρ(h□Vρ​)−h□∂ρVρ​)−∂μ​(hμρ∂ρ​∂ν​Vν)+hμρ∂μ​∂ρ​∂ν​Vν=21​∂ρ​[h∂ρ∂μ​Vμ−h□Vρ−2hμρ∂μ​∂ν​Vν]+hμν∂μ​∂ν​∂ρ​Vρ.​(15)Thus, δL1(1)​+δL2(1)​ is a divergence. Next, we examine the quadratic terms in V,δL1(2)​δL2(2)​​=21​∂ρ​(∂μ​Vν​+∂ν​Vμ​)(∂ν∂μVρ+∂ν∂ρVμ−∂ρ∂μVν)=∂μ​∂ν​Vρ​∂ρ∂μVν,=∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ(∂ρ∂νVν​−∂ν​∂νVρ−∂ν​∂ρVν)=−∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ∂ν​∂νVρ=−∂ν​[∂νVρ∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ]+∂νVρ∂ν​∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ,=−∂ν​[∂νVρ∂ρ​∂μ​Vμ]+∂μ​[∂ν​∂ρ​Vμ∂νVρ]−∂ν​∂ρ​Vμ∂μ​∂νVρ,=∂ρ​[−∂ρVμ∂μ​∂ν​Vν+∂μ​∂ν​Vρ∂μVν]−∂μ​∂ν​Vρ​∂ρ∂μVν.​(16)We observe that δL1(2)​+δL2(2)​ is again a total divergence, which concludes the proof.

Exercise 2. (10 points) We consider a massive spin 1/2 particle described at t=0 by a wave packet with a Gaussian distribution centered at x=0 and of half-width d,Ψ(0,x)=(πd2)3/41​e−x2/(2d2)⎝⎛​22​​22​​00​⎠⎞​.(17)

1.

Find the corresponding solution of the Dirac equation Ψ(t,x). (2 points)

2.

Compute the norm of the solution ∫d3xΨ†(t,x)Ψ(t,x), and verify that it is time independent. (3 points)

3.

Is there a limit in which we can neglect the negative energy solutions? (1 points)

4.

Compute the following integrated current for the Gaussian wave packet, jμ(t)=∫d3xΨˉ(t,x)γμΨ(t,x)(18)and show that its space components vanish, ji(t)=0. (4 points)

Solution: 1. A general solution of the Dirac equation has the formΨ(t,x)=∫(2π)3d3p​r=1,2∑​[br​(p)ur​(p)e−ipx+dr​(p)vr​(p)eipx],(19)with the coefficients br​(p),dr​(p) to be determined, and ur​(p),vr​(p) given by the formulas (2.44) of the lecture notes, namelyur​(p)=p0+m​1​((p0+m)ψr​p⋅σψr​​),vr​(p)=p0+m​1​(p⋅σψr​(p0+m)ψr​​),withψ1​=(10​),ψ2​=(01​).(20)The solution is on mass shell, and so p0=p0(p)=p2+m2​ in this formula. Taking the Fourier transform of the wave function at initial time, we find∫d3xe−ip⋅xΨ(0,x)=(4πd2)3/4e−p2d2/2Ξ,Ξ=22​​⎝⎛​1100​⎠⎞​.(21)Comparing with the Fourier transform of the general solution at t=0, we find the condition(4πd2)3/4e−p2d2/2Ξ=r=1,2∑​[br​(p)ur​(p)+dr​(−p)vr​(−p)].(22)To solve this equation, we use the projection relations (2.45) of the lecture notes, it givesbr​(p)=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/2ur​(p)†Ξ,dr​(−p)=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/2vr​(−p)†Ξ.(23)Introducingξ=22​​(11​)⇒Ξ=(ξ0​),(24)we deduce (recall that σ†=σ),2br​(p)dr​(p)⇒d1​(p)​=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/2p0+m​1​(p0+m)ψr†​ξ=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/2p0+m​22​​,=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/2p0+m​1​ψr†​(p⋅σ)ξ,=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/222​​p0+m​p1−ip2+p3​,d2​(p)=2p0(4πd2)3/4​e−p2d2/222​​p0+m​p1+ip2−p3​.​(25)

2. Let’s denoteN=∫d3xΨ†(t,x)Ψ(t,x)(26)We haveN=∫d3x∫(2π)3d3p1​​∫(2π)3d3p2​​r,s=1∑2​[​eix(p1​−p2​)br∗​(p1​)bs​(p2​)ur​(p1​)†us​(p2​)+e−ix(p1​−p2​)dr∗​(p1​)ds​(p2​)vr​(p1​)†vs​(p2​)+eix(p1​+p2​)br∗​(p1​)ds​(p2​)ur​(p1​)†vs​(p2​)+e−ix(p1​+p2​)dr∗​(p1​)bs​(p2​)vr​(p1​)†us​(p2​)]​(27)The integral over d3x produces delta functions, e.g.∫d3xe−ix(p1​+p2​)∫d3xe−ix(p1​−p2​)​=e−it(p0(p1​)+p0(p2​))∫d3xeix⋅(p1​+p2​)=(2π)3δ(p1​+p2​)e−2itp0(p1​)=e−it(p0(p1​)−p0(p2​))∫d3xeix⋅(p1​−p2​)=(2π)3δ(p1​−p2​).​(28)since p0(p)=p0(−p). This givesN=∫(2π)3d3p​r,s=1∑2​[​br∗​(p)bs​(p)ur​(p)†us​(p)+dr∗​(p)ds​(p)vr​(p)†vs​(p)+e2itp0br∗​(p)ds​(−p)ur​(p)†vs​(−p)+e−2itp0dr∗​(p)bs​(−p)vr​(p)†us​(−p)]​(29)Next, we use the projection relations (2.45), namely3ur†​(p)us​(p)=vr†​(p)vs​(p)=2p0δr,s​,ur†​(p)vs​(−p)=vr†​(p)us​(−p)=0,(30)Most terms disappear, there only remainsN=∫(2π)3d3p​2p0r=1∑2​[br∗​(p)br​(p)+dr∗​(p)dr​(p)].(31)This is indeed time independent. To compute the remaining sum, we recall the previous formulas for the coefficientsbr​(p)=F(p)(p0+m)ξr​,dr​(p)=F(p)(p⋅σξ)r​,withF(p)=2p0(4πd2)3/4​p0+m​e−p2d2/2​.(32)Note that F(p)=F(−p)=F∗(p). Thus, we haver=1∑2​[∣br​(p)∣2+∣dr​(p)∣2]​=F(p)2[(p0+m)2ξ†ξ+ξ†(p⋅σ)2ξ]=F(p)2[(p0+m)2+p2]=2p0(p0+m)F(p)2=2p0(4πd2)3/2​e−p2d2,​(33)using (p⋅σ)2=p2 and ξ†ξ=1. Inserting the coefficients obtained before, we findN=(4πd2)3/2∫(2π)3d3p​e−p2d2=(4πd2)3/2(∫−∞∞​2πdp​e−p2d2)3=1.(34)

3. In the non-relativistic limit ∣p∣≪m, the coefficient in front of the negative energy solution becomes negligible sincebs​(p)dr​(p)​=p0+m(p⋅σξ)r​​≃mpi​≪1.(35)

4. First, we notice thatjμ=∫d3xΨˉ(t,x)γμΨ(t,x)=∫d3xΨ†(t,x)γ0γμΨ(t,x)(36)and so j0=N, which indeed reproduces the formula. Thus, we only need to check the case μ=i. The calculation starts in the same way as before, and using the delta functions, we end up withjμ=∫(2π)3d3p​r,s=1∑2​[​br∗​(p)bs​(p)uˉr​(p)γμus​(p)+dr∗​(p)ds​(p)vˉr​(p)γμvs​(p)+e2itp0br∗​(p)ds​(−p)uˉr​(p)γμvs​(−p)+e−2itp0dr∗​(p)bs​(−p)vˉr​(p)γμus​(−p)]​(37)Let’s decompose jμ=jregμ​+joscμ​ withjregμ​joscμ​​=∫(2π)3d3p​r,s=1∑2​[br∗​(p)bs​(p)uˉr​(p)γμus​(p)+dr∗​(p)ds​(p)vˉr​(p)γμvs​(p)]=∫(2π)3d3p​r,s=1∑2​[e2itp0br∗​(p)ds​(−p)uˉr​(p)γμvs​(−p)+e−2itp0dr∗​(p)bs​(−p)vˉr​(p)γμus​(−p)],​(38)since we have seen that josc0​=0. We need to compute these expressions. In Dirac’s representation, we have the following expressionγ0γi=(0σi​σi0​).(39)Using this expression, we derive4uˉr​(p)γius​(p)uˉr​(p)γivs​(−p)​=vˉr​(p)γivs​(p)=2piδr,s​,=vˉr​(p)γius​(−p)=2p0σr,si​−p0+m2pi​p⋅σr,s​.​(40)The first identity can be used to simplify jregμ​, and we find indeed using our previous calculation (34) of the norm N,jregi​=∫(2π)3d3p​2pir=1∑2​[∣br​(p)∣2+∣dr​(p)∣2]=(4πd2)3/2∫(2π)3d3p​p0pi​e−p2d2(41)By a parity argument, p→−p, we havejregi​=(4πd2)3/221​(∫(2π)3d3p​p0pi​e−p2d2−∫(2π)3d3p​p0pi​e−p2d2)=0.(42)Next, we turn to josc​, and we need to show that it is actually vanishing. We computer,s∑​br∗​(p)σr,sk​ds​(−p)r,s∑​dr∗​(p)σr,sk​bs​(−p)​=−F(p)2(p0+m)ξ†σk(p⋅σ)ξ=−F(p)2(p0+m)plξ†σkσlξ,=F(p)2(p0+m)ξ†(p⋅σ)σkξ=F(p)2(p0+m)plξ†σlσkξ.​(43)Putting everything together, we findjosci​=∫(2π)3d3p​F(p)2(2p0(p0+m)δikpl−2pipkpl)ξ†(−e2itp0σkσl+e−2itp0σlσk)ξ(44)Then, we use−e2itp0σkσl+e−2itp0σlσk=−[σk,σl]cos(2tp0)−isin(2tp0){σk,σl}=−2iεklmσmcos(2tp0)−2iδklsin(2tp0).(45)to rewrite (exploiting the symmetry)josci​​=−4i∫(2π)3d3p​F(p)2(p0(p0+m)(cos(2tp0)εijkpjξ†σkξ−pisin(2tp0))−pip2sin(2tp0))=4i∫(2π)3d3p​F(p)2(m(p0+m)pisin(2tp0)−p0(p0+m)cos(2tp0)εijkpjξ†σkξ).​(46)Finally, we computeξ†σ1ξ=1,ξ†σ2ξ=0,ξ†σ3ξ=0⇒εijkpjξ†σkξ=p∧e1​.(47)It givesjosc​=i(4πd2)3/2∫(2π)3d3p​e−p2d2[(p0)2mp​sin(2tp0)−p0p​∧e1​cos(2tp0)],e1​=⎝⎛​100​⎠⎞​.(48)At this stage, it seems puzzling because the current appears to be purely imaginary. But observe that the integrand G(p) satisfies the symmetry G(−p)=−G(p), and sojosc​=∫−∞∞​G(p)d3p=−∫−∞∞​G(p)d3p=0.(49)Of course, we could have used this argument much earlier, but I believe the full calculation is instructive :

For a general wave packet, these two terms of the current jreg​ and josc​ are non-vanishing. The term josc​, arising due to the presence of negative energy solutions, is at the origin of a phenomenon of oscillations called Zitterbewegung and first observed by Schrödinger.

2Assignment 2

Exercise 1. (10 points) In this exercise, we consider a massive real scalar field, with the mode decompositionΦ(x)=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​(ak​e−ikx+ak†​eikx),[ak​,ak′†​]=2k0δ(3)(k−k′).(54)and [ak​,ak′​]=[ak†​,ak′†​]=0. We also recall the expression of the quantum Hamiltonian, and the corresponding evolution operatorsH=21​∫d3kak†​ak​,U(t)=e−iHt(55)

1.

Compute the adjoint action of the evolution operator on the modes ak​ and ak†​, and deduce that the evolution of the quantum field is indeed given by (2 points) Φ(t,x)=U(t)†Φ(0,x)U(t).(56)

2.

We are interested in the family of coherent states associated to L2 functions f(k):R3→C, and defined as ∣f⟩=exp(∫2k0d3k​f(k)ak†​)∣0⟩.(57)Compute the inner product ⟨f1​∣f2​⟩ of two coherent states associated to different functions f1​ and f2​. Are these states orthogonal? (3 points)

3.

Show that ak​ is diagonal on the state ∣f⟩. What is the corresponding eigenvalue? (3 points)

4.

Show that coherent states remain coherent under time evolution, and more specifically (2 points) U(t)∣f⟩=∣ft​⟩,withft​(k)=e−itk2+m2​f(k).(58)

Solutions:

1. We use the formula for two operators A and B,eABe−A=eadA​B=n=0∑∞​n!(adA​)n​B,adA​B=[A,B].(59)We have[H,ak​][H,ak†​]​=21​∫2k′0d3k′​[ak′†​ak′​,ak​]=−21​∫2k′0d3k′​2k0δ(3)(k−k′)ak′​=−k0ak​,=21​∫2k′0d3k′​[ak′†​ak′​,ak†​]=21​∫2k′0d3k′​2k0δ(3)(k−k′)ak′†​=k0ak†​​(60)and so[itH,ak​][itH,ak†​]​=−itk0ak​⇒(aditH​)nak​=(−itk0)nak​⇒U(t)†ak​U(t)=eitHak​e−itH=e−itk0ak​,=itk0ak​⇒(aditH​)nak†​=(itk0)nak†​⇒U(t)†ak†​U(t)=eitHak†​e−itH=eitk0ak†​,​(61)since H†=H and so U(t)†=U(t)−1=U(−t). Thus, we findU(t)†Φ(0,x)U(t)​=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​U(t)†(ak​e−ik⋅x+ak†​eik⋅x)U(t)=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​(U(t)†ak​U(t)eik⋅x+U(t)†ak†​U(t)e−ik⋅x)=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​(e−ik0tak​eik⋅x+eik0tak†​e−ik⋅x)=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​(e−ikxak​+ak†​eikx)=Φ(t,x).​(62)

2. Expanding the exponentials, we have⟨f1​∣f2​⟩=n,m=0∑∞​n!m!1​∫α=1∏n​[f1∗​(kα​)2kα0​d3kα​​]β=1∏m​[f2​(kβ′​)2kβ′0​d3kβ′​​]⟨0∣ak1​​⋯akn​​ak1′​†​⋯akm′​†​∣0⟩.(63)LetCn,m​=⟨0∣ak1​​⋯akn​​ak1′​†​⋯akm′​†​∣0⟩.(64)By induction, one can show thatCn,m​(k1​,⋯,kn​∣k1′​,⋯,km′​)=δn,m​σ∈Sn​∑​α=1∏n​2kα0​δ(3)(kα​−kσ(α)′​).(65)Let’s first consider the case n=m. We obviously have C00​=1, and using the commutation relations, we find C11​=2k10​δ(3)(k1​−k1′​). The first non-trivial case isC22​(k1​,k2​∣k1′​,k2′​)​=⟨0∣ak1​​ak2​​ak1′​†​ak2′​†​∣0⟩=2k20​δ(3)(k2​−k1′​)⟨0∣ak1​​ak2′​†​∣0⟩+2k20​δ(3)(k2​−k2′​)⟨0∣ak1​​ak1′​†​∣0⟩=2k20​δ(3)(k2​−k1′​)C11​(k1​∣k2′​)+2k20​δ(3)(k2​−k2′​)C11​(k1​∣k1′​)​(66)where the second line is obtained by moving ak2​​ to the right using the commutator until it reaches the state ∣0⟩ where the corresponding term vanishes since ak2​​∣0⟩=0. Repeating this argument, we haveCnn​(k1​,⋯,kn​∣k1′​,⋯,kn′​)=β=1∑n​2kn(0)​δ(3)(kn​−kβ​)Cn−1 n−1​(k1​,⋯,kn−1​∣k1′​,⋯,kα′​​,⋯,kn′​).(67)Thus, by induction we haveCnn​(k1​,⋯,kn​∣k1′​,⋯,kn′​)​=β=1∑n​2kn(0)​δ(3)(kn​−kβ​)σ∈Sn−1​∑​α=1∏n−1​2kα0​δ(3)(kα​−kσ(α)′​)=σ∈Sn​∑​α=1∏n​2kα0​δ(3)(kα​−kσ(α)′​)​(68)denoting β=σ(n). It remains to show the orthogonality Cn,m​∝δn,m​, this is done by noticing that if n>m or n<m the commutation procedure used above will terminate with extra insertions of a or a†, and so the corresponding correlator should vanish. For instance,C21​(k1​,k2​∣k1′​)C12​(k1​∣k1′​,k2′​)​=⟨0∣ak1​​ak2​​ak1′​†​∣0⟩=2k20​δ(3)(k2​−k1′​)⟨0∣ak1​​∣0⟩=0,=⟨0∣ak1​​ak1′​†​ak2′​†​∣0⟩=2k10​δ(3)(k1​−k1′​)⟨0∣ak2′​†​∣0⟩+2k10​δ(3)(k1​−k2′​)⟨0∣ak1′​†​∣0⟩=0.​(69)Coming back to the expression of the inner product, and inserting our result for Cnn​, we find⟨f1​∣f2​⟩​=n,m=0∑∞​n!m!1​∫α=1∏n​[f1∗​(kα​)2kα0​d3kα​​]β=1∏m​[f2​(kβ′​)2kβ′0​d3kβ′​​]δn,m​σ∈Sn​∑​α=1∏n​2kα0​δ(3)(kα​−kσ(α)′​)=n=0∑∞​(n!)21​σ∈Sn​∑​∫α=1∏n​[f1∗​(kα​)2kα0​d3kα​​]β=1∏n​[f2​(kβ′​)2kβ′0​d3kβ′​​]α=1∏n​[2kα0​δ(3)(kα​−kσ(α)′​)]=n=0∑∞​n!1​∫α=1∏n​[f1∗​(kα​)2kα0​d3kα​​]β=1∏n​[f2​(kβ′​)2kβ′0​d3kβ′​​]δn,m​α=1∏n​[2kα0​δ(3)(kα​−kα′​)]=n=0∑∞​n!1​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f1∗​(kα​)f2​(kα​)]=exp(∫2k0d3k​f1∗​(k)f2​(k))​(70)by exploiting the invariance under permutation of the integral. In general, the integral inside the exponential is non-vanishing and the states are not orthogonal.

3. Let’s first compute by induction[ak​,ak1​†​⋯akn​†​]=α=1∑n​2kα(0)​δ(3)(k−kα​)ak1​†​⋯akα​†​​⋯akn​†​,(71)and since ak​∣0⟩=0, we deduceak​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]ak1​†​⋯akn​†​∣0⟩​=β=1∑n​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]2kβ(0)​δ(3)(k−kβ​)ak1​†​⋯akβ​†​​⋯akn​†​∣0⟩=n∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]2kn(0)​δ(3)(k−kn​)ak1​†​⋯akn−1​†​∣0⟩=nf(k)∫α=1∏n−1​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]ak1​†​⋯akn−1​†​∣0⟩,​(72)since we can always commute the operators and relabel the variables to take β=n. We deduce thatak​∣f⟩​=n=0∑∞​n!1​ak​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]ak1​†​⋯akn​†​∣0⟩=n=1∑∞​(n−1)!1​f(k)∫α=1∏n−1​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]ak1​†​⋯akn−1​†​∣0⟩=f(k)∣f⟩.​(73)Thus ak​ is diagonal on the states ∣f⟩ with eigenvalue f(k).

4. This calculation is very similar to the case of the field solved in question one. Using the result on the time evolution of the modes, we can write downU(t)∣f⟩​=n=0∑∞​n!1​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]U(t)ak1​†​⋯akn​†​∣0⟩=n=0∑∞​n!1​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]U(t)ak1​†​U(t)−1U(t)ak2​†​U(t)−1⋯U(t)akn​†​U(t)−1U(t)∣0⟩=n=0∑∞​n!1​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​f(kα​)]e−ik10​tak1​†​e−ik20​tak2​†​⋯e−ikn0​takn​†​∣0⟩=n=0∑∞​n!1​∫α=1∏n​[2kα0​d3kα​​e−ikα0​tf(kα​)]ak1​†​ak2​†​⋯akn​†​∣0⟩=∣ft​⟩,​(74)where we used U(t)∣0⟩=∣0⟩ since H∣0⟩=0.

Exercise 2. (10 points) In this exercise, we study both the classical and quantum Dirac spinor fields of mass m.

1.

Let σ=(σ1,σ2,σ3) be the vector of Pauli matrices and k=(k1,k2,k3) the momentum vector. Find two orthonormal eigenvectors of the matrix k⋅σ with eigenvalues ∣k∣ and −∣k∣. In the following, we will denote them φ1​(k) and φ2​(k) respectively. (1 point)

2.

We introduce the following 4-vector of polarization, Ur​(k)=k0+m​1​((k0+m)φr​(k)k⋅σφr​(k)​),Vr​(k)=k0+m​1​(k⋅σφr​(k)(k0+m)φr​(k)​),(75)and the classical field Ψ(x)=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(Ur​(k)brk​e−ikx+Vr​(k)drk∗​eikx),(76)with arbitrary modes brk​ and drk∗​ determined from initial conditions. Explain why Ψ(x) satisfies the Dirac equation. (1 point)

3.

Show that the following projection relations hold (1 point) Ur†​(k)Us​(k)=Vr†​(k)Vs​(k)=2k0δr,s​,Ur†​(k)Vs​(−k)=Vr†​(k)Us​(−k)=0.(77)

4.

We define the helicity operator Sk​=∣k∣k⋅Σ​ where Σ is the vector of 4×4 matrices Σ=(σ0​0σ​). Show that Ur​(k) and Vr​(k) are eigenvectors of Sk​ with eigenvalues (−1)r+1. (1 point)

5.

We now introduce a quantum Dirac field with the same polarization vectors, Ψ(x)=(2π)3/21​∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(Ur​(k)brk​e−ikx+Vr​(k)drk†​eikx),(78)with the modes satisfying the anticommutation relations {brk​,bsk′†​}={drk​,dsk′†​}=2k0δ(3)(k−k′)δr,s​ (other anticommutators being trivial). The quantum helicity operator can be obtained as a projection of the Pauli-Lubanski operator on the direction of momentum. It leads to the following expression S^=2−i​∫d3x:Ψ†(x)Σ⋅∇^Ψ(x):,(79)where the differential operator ∇^ acts as follows on the Dirac field, ∇^Ψ(x)=(2π)3/2i​∫2k0d3k​∣k∣k​r=1,2∑​(Ur​(k)brk​e−ikx−Vr​(k)drk†​eikx)(80)Show that in our polarization basis, the helicity operator simplifies into (3 points) S^=21​∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(−)r+1(brk†​brk​+drk†​drk​).(81)

6.

We consider a state with one particle and one antiparticle with the same momentum and independent polarizations, ∣11ˉrs⟩=brk†​dsk†​∣0⟩.(82)Compute the energy, momentum, helicity and U(1) charge of this state. (3 points)

Solutions:

1. Solutions might differ by a phase, but using your favorite method you should findφ1​(k)=2∣k∣(∣k∣−k3)​1​(k1−ik2−k3+∣k∣​),φ2​(k)=2∣k∣(∣k∣+k3)​1​(k1−ik2−k3−∣k∣​).(83)Note that we have indeed φr†​φs​=δr,s​.

2. Using the Fourier transform, we have shown in class that solutions of the Dirac equations are of the form (23) where polarization vectors Ur​(k) and Vr​(k) must satisfy the equations(k−m)Ur​(k)=0,(k+m)Vr​(k)=0.(84)Then, we have shown that the solutions of these equations are given by vectors of the formUr​(k)=k0+m​1​((k0+m)ψr​k⋅σψr​​),Vr​(k)=k0+m​1​(k⋅σχr​(k0+m)χr​​).(85)where ψr​ (and χr​) are two arbitrary linearly independent two dimensional vectors. The choice ψr​=χr​=φr​(k) is just a particular case.

3. We use the same method as seen in class, exploiting the fact that φr†​φs​=δr,s​, σ†=σ and the mass shell condition m2=(k0)2−k2. For instance,Ur​(k)†Us​(k)​=k0+m1​[φr​(k)†(k0+m)2φs​(k)+φr​(k)†(k⋅σ)2φs​(k)]=k0+m1​[(k0+m)2+k2]φr​(k)†φs​(k)=2k0δr,s​,​(86)since (k⋅σ)2=kikjσiσj=kikjδi,j​=k2, andUr​(k)†Vs​(−k)=k0+m1​[−φr​(k)†(k0+m)(k⋅σ)φs​(k)+φr​(k)†(k⋅σ)(k0+m)φs​(k)]=0.(87)The other two relations are obtained in the same way.

4. Using the property (k⋅σ)φr​(k)=(−)r+1∣k∣ and (k⋅σ)2=k2, we compute(k⋅Σ)Ur​(k)​=k0+m​1​(k⋅σ0​0k⋅σ​)((k0+m)φr​(k)k⋅σφr​(k)​)=k0+m​1​((k0+m)k⋅σφr​(k)k2φr​(k)​)=k0+m​(−)r+1∣k∣​((k0+m)φr​(k)(k⋅σ)φr​(k)​)=(−)r+1∣k∣Ur​(k)⇒Sk​Ur​(k)=(−)r+1Ur​(k).​(88)The calculation is exactly the same for Vr​(k).

5. This calculation is very similar to what we have been doing in class, so we will be brief. From the expression of the operators S^ and ∇^, we findS^=2(2π)31​∫d3x∫2k0d3k​∫2k′0d3k′​r,s=1,2∑​:(Ur​(k)†brk†​eikx+Vr​(k)†drk​e−ikx)∣k′∣k′⋅Σ​(Us​(k′)bsk′​e−ik′x−Vs​(k′)dsk′†​eik′x):.(89)We start by performing the d3x integration, it produces delta functions (see Assignment 1),S^=21​∫2k0d3k​∫2k′0d3k′​r,s=1,2∑​[​δ(3)(k−k′)(Ur​(k)†∣k′∣k′⋅Σ​Us​(k′):brk†​bsk′​:−Vr​(k)†∣k′∣k′⋅Σ​Vs​(k′):drk​dsk′†​:)+δ(3)(k+k′)(−e2ik0tUr​(k)†∣k′∣k′⋅Σ​Vs​(k′):brk†​dsk′†​:+e−2ik0tVr​(k)†∣k′∣k′⋅Σ​Us​(k′):drk​bsk′​:)].​(90)Then, we use the fact that polarization vectors are eigenvectors of the operator Sk′​ with eigenvalue (−1)s+1, and soS^=21​∫2k0d3k​∫2k′0d3k′​r,s=1,2∑​(−1)s+1[​δ(3)(k−k′)(Ur​(k)†Us​(k′):brk†​bsk′​:−Vr​(k)†Vs​(k′):drk​dsk′†​:)+δ(3)(k+k′)(−e2ik0tUr​(k)†Vs​(k′):brk†​dsk′†​:+e−2ik0tVr​(k)†Us​(k′):drk​bsk′​:)]​(91)The delta functions can be used to eliminate one of the two integrations,S^=21​∫(2k0)2d3k​r,s=1,2∑​(−1)s+1[​Ur​(k)†Us​(k):brk†​bsk​:−Vr​(k)†Vs​(k):drk​dsk†​:−e2ik0tUr​(k)†Vs​(−k):brk†​ds−k†​:+e−2ik0tVr​(k)†Us​(−k):drk​bs−k​:]​(92)Finally, using the projection relations of the polarization vectors, and then normal-order relations, we find the expected resultS^​=21​∫(2k0)2d3k​r,s=1,2∑​(−1)s+12k0δr,s​(:brk†​bsk​:−:drk​dsk†​:)=21​∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(−1)r+1(:brk†​brk​:−:drk​drk†​:)=21​∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(−1)r+1(brk†​brk​+drk†​drk​).​(93)

6. Let’s introduce the number of particles operators Nrk​=brk†​brk​, Nˉrk​=drk†​drk​, then we can show that[Nrk​,bsk′†​][Nrk​,dsk′†​]​=brk†​brk​bsk′†​−bsk′†​brk†​brk​=2k0δr,s​δ(3)(k−k′)brk†​−brk†​bsk′†​brk​−bsk′†​brk†​brk​=2k0δr,s​δ(3)(k−k′)brk†​,=brk†​brk​dsk′†​−dsk′†​brk†​brk​=−brk†​dsk′†​brk​−dsk′†​brk†​brk​=0,​(94)and, in the same way, exchanging b and d,[Nˉrk​,bsk′†​]=0,[Nˉrk​,dsk′†​]=2k0δr,s​δ(3)(k−k′)drk†​.(95)Note also that Nrk​∣0⟩=Nˉrk​∣0⟩=0. Then, notice that all our operators can actually be expressed in terms of these number operators,Pμ=∫2k0d3k​kμr=1,2∑​(Nrk​+Nˉrk​),S^=21​∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(−)r+1(Nrk​+Nˉrk​),Q=∫2k0d3k​r=1,2∑​(Nrk​−Nˉrk​).(96)We deduce that the vacuum satisfies Pμ∣0⟩=S^∣0⟩=Q∣0⟩, and creation operators[Pμ,brk†​][Pμ,drk†​]​=kμbrk†​,=kμdrk†​,​[S^,brk†​][S^,drk†​]​=2(−)r+1​brk†​,=2(−)r+1​drk†​,​[Q,brk†​][Q,drk†​]​=brk†​,=−drk†​,​(97)As a result, we havePμ∣11ˉrs⟩​=Pμbrk†​dsk†​∣0⟩=[Pμ,brk†​]dsk†​∣0⟩+brk†​[Pμ,dsk†​]∣0⟩+brk†​dsk†​Pμ∣0⟩=kμbrk†​dsk†​∣0⟩+kμbrk†​dsk†​∣0⟩=2kμ∣11ˉrs⟩.​(98)In the same way, we findS^∣11ˉrs⟩=21​((−1)r+1+(−1)s+1)∣11ˉrs⟩,Q∣11ˉrs⟩=0.(99)Thus, we find that this state has momentum 2k, energy 2k0=2m2+k2​, U(1) charge zero, and helicity that depends on r,s, more preciselyS^∣11ˉ11⟩=∣11ˉ11⟩,S^∣11ˉ12⟩=0,S^∣11ˉ21⟩=0,S^∣11ˉ22⟩=−∣11ˉ22⟩.(100)
